newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb police rough up protesters, courts hit Zajedno.
newsitem.headline: Serb police rough up protesters, courts hit Zajedno.

text.p: Serbian riot police roughed up several pro-democracy demonstrators in Belgrade while courts dealt two serious blows to government opponents in their bid to reinstate November election results.

Baton-wielding riot police, who have set up security cordons day after day for more than two months, waded into a handful of demonstrators who were among a group of several hundred people marching through Belgrade on Monday night.

According to Reuters television film, the policemen hit several demonstrators with batons and hit and pushed one woman to the pavement. She was driven away in an ambulance but her identity and the extent of her injuries were unknown.

Violent incidents have been rare in recent weeks in the two-month-long protest campaign by pro-democracy demonstrators demanding that the government reinstate annulled results of November municipal elections in which the Zajedno (Together) coalition won Belgrade and 13 other towns.
But Dr Slobodan Ivanovic of the private Belgrade clinic Anlave told Reuters that demonstrators had been injured in other parts of the city as well.
He said the clinic's ambulance had transported two men suffering from head injuries and three others, including two women, who had suffered injuries to their legs or arms.
Independent radios B-92 and Radio Index reported beatings of demonstrators in the suburb of Banovo Brdo.
Thousands of students kept up a non-stop demonstration into a second night as riot police refused to budge and let them march around the centre of Belgrade.

The students, who support opposition demands that autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic reinstate the election results, blew whistles and danced late into the night while a cordon of hundreds of helmeted riot police stopped them from marching through the city. The police had let them march for three nights last week.
One young woman student danced for 17 hours while a local independent radio station quoted a policeman as saying: "Oh, let them walk where they want, after all they're all our children."
The students brought in tents to shelter them from the rain but were only able to set up one, with great difficulty, people attending the demonstration said.

The marathon demonstration continued on the same day that the opposition, which has received strong international support to have the election results reinstated, was dealt two blows by the Serbian courts.
The municipal court in Belgrade suspended an electoral commission decision reversing a court ruling and awarding victory in the capital to the Zajedno coalition.

The Belgrade court, acting on appeals by Milosevic's ruling Socialist (SPS) party and the rightist Serbian Radical Party (SRS), ducked out of responsibility and asked the Supreme Court to rule on which court had jurisdiction.
The Supreme Court -- which diplomats say is not immune to Socialist power politics --- ruled that Milosevic's party had won 35 seats and Zajedno 29 in the local assembly of the western town of Sabac.

Both decisions flouted the findings of an inquiry by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) that verified the opposition coalition's claim to have won Belgrade, Sabac and 12 other towns where the Socialists annulled elections in November claiming "irregularities".
The European Union expressed its full support for Zajedno on Monday and demanded the Belgrade authorities recognise the opposition victories.
Western governments have told Milosevic he will not get economic reconstruction aid unless his government admits election losses and embarks on broader democratic reform.
